text: Manny Díaz Jr., born on March 2, 1973, is an American politician currently serving as the president of the University of West Florida. He served as the 28th education commissioner of Florida from 2022 to 2025. A Republican, Díaz represented the 36th district in the Florida Senate from 2018 to 2022, which includes the Hialeah area in northwest Miami-Dade County. He previously served three terms in the Florida House of Representatives from 2012 to 2018, representing parts of Hialeah and Northwest Miami-Dade County. Díaz was born in Hialeah, graduated from Miami Springs High School, and earned a degree in human resources from St. Thomas University in 1994. He later obtained a master's degree in educational leadership from Nova Southeastern University in 1998. In 2006, he completed the Harvard University Graduate School of Education Principal's Summer Institute as part of the Superintendent's Urban Principal Initiative. He began his career as a teacher and baseball coach at Miami Springs High School, teaching social studies at Hialeah-Miami Lakes High School from 1995 to 1999, where he served as assistant principal for eight years. From 2013 to 2019, he was assistant principal at George T. Baker Aviation School, a public vocational school near Miami International Airport. Díaz denied allegations of discussing drug use or making inappropriate comments to a female student during his 1990s teaching career, attributing them to political attacks by a Democratic marketing consultant. In 2012, he filed for bankruptcy, citing $1.3 million in debts. From 2013 to 2022, he worked for Doral College, a private college affiliated with the for-profit Academica charter school operator founded by Fernando Zulueta, serving as its chief operating officer for most of that time; the institution failed to receive accreditation from the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools and eventually received accreditation from a minor accreditor. On July 14, 2025, Díaz was named interim president of the University of West Florida following the resignation of Martha Dunagin Saunders; during his interim tenure, he fired the university's general counsel after she objected to his hiring of Lawson Huck Gonzalez, a Ron DeSantis-linked law firm, as outside counsel for the presidential search. On January 8, 2026, Díaz was officially appointed president of the University of West Florida with a starting salary of $950,000; the selection process faced allegations of procedural irregularities, and contract requirements were changed to accommodate his lack of a doctoral degree. His advocacy for charter school expansion was also a point of concern. In 2010, Díaz ran for the Miami-Dade County School Board but lost in the primary to Perla Tabares Hantman, receiving 39% of the vote compared to her 61%. In 2012, after Florida House districts were reconfigured, he ran in the newly created 103rd district in the Republican primary against Renier Díaz de la Portilla and Alfredo Naredo-Acosta, winning 55% of the vote to their 39% and 6%, respectively, and faced only write-in opposition in the general election, winning by a wide margin. He was re-elected in 2014 and 2016. During his time in the legislature, he chaired the Choice and Innovation and K-12 Appropriations committee and was a key member of Representative José R. Oliva's team, who later became the second Cuban-American speaker of the Florida House. In 2018, Díaz was elected to the Florida Senate District 36, defeating Democrat David Perez 54.1% to 45.9%, with his re-election receiving substantial funding from health care and education companies. He chaired the Senate Education committee from 2018 to 2020 and the Senate Health Policy committee from 2020 to 2022. During the 2022 legislative session, he was the only Republican to vote against the congressional redistricting plan, indicating his alignment with Governor Ron DeSantis. On June 1, 2022, he assumed office as Education Commissioner after Richard Corcoran stepped down. In 2024, the Florida Board of Governors eliminated sociology as a core course at its public universities, a move Díaz defended by stating that sociology had been "hijacked by left-wing activists" and no longer served its intended purpose as a general knowledge course. While in the legislature, he sponsored legislation allowing more private online education providers, some from outside Florida, to offer classes to public school students, permitting students to take classes in public virtual schools in other counties, and requiring the Florida Department of Education to create a catalogue of online offerings. In 2017, he rejected allegations of conflict of interest when he co-sponsored, with Richard Corcoran and Michael Bileca, legislation directing $140 million in public funds to charter schools, noting that all three men and their wives were involved in the charter school industry. He sponsored the 2019 Family Empowerment Scholarship legislation and a 2020 bill that significantly expanded publicly-funded vouchers for private schools, widely regarded as the largest expansion of school choice in the nation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Díaz opposed vaccine requirements for students and in 2021 expressed interest in reviewing additional vaccine mandates, such as for mumps and measles; as of September 2021, he had not been vaccinated against COVID-19. In 2022, he sponsored SB148/HB7, an "anti-woke" bill supported by Governor Ron DeSantis; after being signed into law in April 2022, Chief U.S. District Judge Mark E. Walker blocked key provisions in November 2022, calling the law "positively dystopian." Díaz was a four-year letterman in college baseball at St. Thomas University, playing under head coach Al Avila. His second wife, Jennifer, worked in Miami-Dade Public Schools and Miami-Dade charter schools; they married on December 11, 2010. She previously served as vice-chair of the governing board of the Tallahassee Classical School, affiliated with Hillsdale College. They have three children; Díaz's son Dominic, from his first marriage to Linet Gonzalez, played baseball at Longwood University.
